_comment: Plain-language definitions of AI terms. Surfaced site-wide via tooltip/hover on matching terms. Editable by non-engineers. `term` is what users see; `aliases` are alternate spellings/forms that should also trigger the tooltip.

terms.definition: When an AI tool produces information that sounds confident and plausible but is actually false, made up, or not supported by any real source. Always verify factual claims independently.
The instructions or question you give an AI tool. A clear, specific prompt with the right context usually produces a better, more useful response.
The practice of writing and refining prompts to get more accurate, relevant, or well-formatted results from an AI tool.
The maximum amount of text an AI tool can consider at once — including your prompt and its response. Very long documents may exceed it, causing the tool to 'forget' earlier parts.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation: a technique where an AI tool looks up relevant information from a specific set of documents and uses it to answer, rather than relying only on what it learned during training. This grounds answers in real sources and reduces hallucination.
The underlying AI system (such as the model behind U-M GPT) trained on large amounts of text to predict and generate human-like language.
The text and information an AI model learned from. Models generally do not know about events after their training cutoff and may reflect biases present in that data.
Systematic unfairness in AI outputs that can arise from patterns in training data — for example, skewed or stereotyped results for certain groups. Review outputs critically for fairness.
Another word for hallucination — when an AI fills gaps with invented but confident-sounding details.
Further training a base AI model on additional, specialized data so it performs better on a specific task or domain. ATLAS's Advisor is prompt-based, not fine-tuned.
The small chunks of text (roughly word-pieces) an AI model reads and generates. Context windows and usage are often measured in tokens.
How U-M categorizes information by sensitivity (for example, public vs. confidential or regulated). The classification determines which tools and handling practices are allowed.
